subsubtopic: SUGGESTED REFERENCE OF NEW EXPANSION PLANS FOR VANCOUVER TO PLANNING COMMITTEE-MOTION UNDER S.O.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity which concerns the proposed expansion of the Vancouver International Airport. In view of the recent statements by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) that this expansion may take place within the Sea Island dyke, in view of the fact that this proposal has not been referred to the airport planning committee which had previously vigorously opposed the airport expansion, and in view of the fact that such expansion will trigger additional non-co-ordinated development in the Fraser estuary, I would move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That this new proposal be referred to the airport planning committee and that a moratorium be placed on further development until proper studies not only of the airport expansion but all expansion in the Fraser estuafy be completed.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLEGED STATEMENT BY MINISTER "ORION" WAS NOT THE RIGHT AIRCRAFT-REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is addressed to the Prime Minister and arises out of the dreadful situation in which we find ourselves in the matter of re-equipping the Canadian Armed Forces, particularly having regard to the difficulties in which the country and the government have been placed by his Minister of National Defence. I want to ask the Prime Minister with respect to a quote attributed to the Minister of National Defence in the press today, in which he said-I am quoting-that "he did not necessarily think the Orion was the right one in the first place", referring to a long range patrol aircraft. If this report is correct, can the Prime Minister indicate whether he has conferred with the Minister of National Defence, what is the state of mind of that minister in respect of the matter, and why did the deal go as far as it did if this transaction involving the Orion and its concept did not have the full support of the Minister of National Defence, as he is now supposed to have said?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: ALLEGED STATEMENT BY MINISTER "ORION" WAS NOT THE RIGHT AIRCRAFT-REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is asking me if a quotation in a newspaper is correct. I have seen the quotation but I do not know if it is a correct one. I can see many ways of explaining the thought that might be behind such a quote. There were many options before the Cabinet, some of which were much more costly than the one we eventually

May 25, 1976
Oral Questions
chose. Perhaps the minister had in mind that there were better deals if we had more money. We certainly made the decision, for the money we could dispose of over a period of time, which represented the best possible deal.

subtopic: REASON FOR DELAY IN DECIDING ON ALTERNATIVE TO THE "ORION"

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: REASON FOR DELAY IN DECIDING ON ALTERNATIVE TO THE "ORION"
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I was not so much concerned about the Prime Minister having seen the press reports as I was about the Prime Minister having seen his Minister of National Defence. The minister is also reported to have said there are at least six possible alternatives of LRPA, and he has hopes of making a decision by the fall. Since all of these other options must have been thoroughly examined in the past before the Lockheed LRPA was finally decided upon, would the Prime Minister explain why we now have to wait until the fall before a new decision is reached? Are there any other elements that were not present when the other options were discarded that would make one of these other six or so alternatives of which the minister has spoken now relevant?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: REASON FOR DELAY IN DECIDING ON ALTERNATIVE TO THE "ORION"
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there were, indeed, many options looked at, and the fact of having chosen one means that the other options fell by the wayside. The conditions, submissions and tenderings which were put forward by the other companies would certainly not apply at the present time. We would have to reassess the kind of options the various other companies would be making to see whether they were still within the price range we were interested in and to see what effects inflation or other technological change might have had on them, and then make a new choice. It does not seem to be complicated.

speakeroldname: Hon. James Richardson (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: ALLEGED STATEMENT BY MINISTER "ORION" WAS NOT THE RIGHT AIRCRAFT-REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION

subtopic: REASON FOR ANNOUNCING PURCHASE OF LEOPARD TANKS AT NATO MEETING-REQUEST FOR ESTIMATE OF COST

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it was reported over the weekend at the meeting of NATO foreign ministers in Oslo, that the Secretary of State for External Affairs announced that Canada is going to purchase 128 Leopard Mark I tanks for use in Canada and Europe. Today it was reported that the West German Minister of Defence has welcomed this decision. Can the Minister of National Defence confirm this decision, and also offer some explanation of why it was decided to have such an important announcement made abroad by the Secretary of State for External Affairs rather than have it made in this House by the Minister of National Defence?

I can confirm that the negotiations with the German government for the purchase of the Leopard I are proceeding satisfactorily, but there are a number of matters still to be concluded, and I think that fact was contained in the statement made. REASON MINISTER MADE COMMITMENT TO LOCKHEED IN VIEW OF UNCERTAINTY ABOUT FINANCING
speechtext: Well, Mr. Speaker, I will have to read the transcript because the answer makes even less sense than usual. Following this answer, and with regard to the report in the Toronto Star of Saturday in which it is stated that the minister said that a "one man to one man verbal conversation" is by no means sufficient when one negotiates a contract involving hundreds of millions of dollars, may I say that I agree with him entirely. However, I should like to ask him if he believes that why would he send a telex committing the government to this deal last December when they had no commitment at that time for front-end financing for which he is responsible, and why more particularly after four further months did he on behalf of the government sign another contract with Lockheed committing the government to pay some $16 million without the assurance at that time that they would have the front-end financing.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean-Pierre Goyer (Minister of Supply and Services):
subtopic: REASON MINISTER MADE COMMITMENT TO LOCKHEED IN VIEW OF UNCERTAINTY ABOUT FINANCING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the hon. member will read today's debates of the House, I suggest to him that he also go over those of the last few months. As a matter of fact, the Minister of National Defence indicated that an official of his department had talked with an official of Lockheed concerning a possible means of financing the contract. In fact, as I told the House in December, we authorized Lockheed to undertake preliminary work for the contract. We authorized Lockheed to undertake preliminary work for the contract to protect the terms and conditions we had negotiated with it and which we regarded as a good deal. Our expenses with the Lockheed Corporation were not to exceed $16 million.

May 25, 1976
Oral Questions
have had some from some parts of the province of Quebec because producers in parts of Quebec recognize their responsibility toward making this program a success, and we are weighing it on those merits. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a supplementary.
Since industrial milk producers committed themselves to reduce their production by 12 per cent and the government requested 15 per cent last March or April, and since it seems now that the government requests 20 per cent reductions of their 1973-74 quotas, would the minister indicate whether this rumour is well founded?

We are

PROPOSED CHECK-OFF SYSTEM TO SUPPORT RESEARCH-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct a question to the minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board. speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subtopic: PROPOSED CHECK-OFF SYSTEM TO SUPPORT RESEARCH-GOVERNMENT POSITION

subtopic: PROPOSED CHECK-OFF SYSTEM TO SUPPORT RESEARCH-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Can the minister give us a time frame in which we can expect a plebiscite in connection with a check-off system; if so, can the minister assure the House that possible legislation would be brought to parliament in the next session?

May 25, 1976

subsubtopic: PROPOSED RATE CHANGES ON RAPESEED AND RAPESEED PRODUCTS-VIEWS OF PROVINCES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Transport. May I ask the minister if he has received a response from the premiers of the prairie provinces and their ministers of transport to his May 6 Telex in regard to the order in council dated May 13 which advanced the new freight rate proposal with respect to rapeseed and rapeseed products which I might say further aggravates the anomaly between raw rapeseed and processed rapeseed? Could the minister indicate the nature of his reply and if he has received a response from the premiers?

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: PROPOSED RATE CHANGES ON RAPESEED AND RAPESEED PRODUCTS-VIEWS OF PROVINCES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there is a sequence of telegrams moving back and forth and there may have been an interim reply to some of the points in my May 6 telegram. So far as I know, there has not been a reply to my latest telegram. As the hon. member knows, my reaction was to hold the level of rates on rapeseed oil at the lowest rate legally possible under the existing law, namely the compensatory rate. The discrepancy between rates or the anomaly to which the hon. member refers is solely due to the fact that the rapeseed is at a much lower rate than that, even though the oil is at a rate well below cost.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED RATE CHANGES ON RAPESEED AND RAPESEED PRODUCTS-VIEWS OF PROVINCES
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. The minister failed to acknowledge the fact that the rate for rapeseed meal has been adjusted upwards and that has placed a severe hardship on the processing industry in western Canada. In light of the fact that we now find that processors in western Canada are forced to suspend their rapeseed growing contracts with producers as a result of the new freight rate proposal, does the minister not consider his unilateral dictatorial action somewhat premature, having regard to the fact that we have a Stave-ly commission and a Hall commission studying all aspects of costing and grain transportation in western Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: PROPOSED RATE CHANGES ON RAPESEED AND RAPESEED PRODUCTS-VIEWS OF PROVINCES

In view of the fact that the appeal process from the CTC decision has in effect taken eight or nine months or more, I can hardly join with the hon. member in thinking that we were in any great rush.

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subtopic: EFFECT ON INDUSTRY OF RATES ON RAPESEED-POSSIBILITY OF CHANGE IN CROWSNEST FREIGHT RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have assessed the impact in relation to processing and, of course, it is true that differences in rates between raw materials and processed materials lead to the movement of the raw material as against the processing and movement of that material. I will be before the House in the next session with legislation to begin to deal more effectively with that whole issue in general. Of course, what I have done in relation to the western premiers or their transport ministers has been to ask them to please be honest enough to say so if what they mean is that they want a subsidy from other freight or from other taxpayers on the rapeseed, instead of hiding behind the argument of equity. Equity, of course, leading to the processing of a product can occur whatever the level of the rate.
I have been pointing out to the premiers that they can hardly expect a rate as far below cost as the Crow rate is, to be applied to other goods today such as oil and beef. In both cases, we get the discrepancy of movement of the seed or the grain instead of the movement of the product. What I want from them is honesty to recognize that if there is equity to be obtained it can be obtained, and perhaps even at a below cost level, but if what they are really insisting upon is subsidies in a new area on particular products, they should be honest enough to say so.

1.	Has Mr. Andrew Cohen, former Executive Assistant to the Secretary of State, been commissioned to do any research work in France on behalf of the Department and, if so (a) for what purpose (b) what fees or other remuneration will he receive?
2.	In what location is such work to be undertaken and what is the duration of the Commission?
3.	What agencies of the government or any other government or the United Nations or any agency thereof have carried on similar research?

speakeroldname: Hon. James Hugh Faulkner (Secretary of State):
subsubtopic: MR. ANDREW COHEN
speechtext:
In so
far as the Department of the Secretary of State is concerned: 1. Mr. Cohen is under contract to do research work in Western Europe. He is living in France, but his work will not be confined to that country, (a) Mr. Cohen is to prepare for the Department of the Secretary of State a report on the extent and nature of government involvement, in a number of West European countries, in the film and publishing fields with respect to: (1) legislation. (2) funding mechanisms. (3) existence of special agencies for promotion of film and publishing on the marketing of books and films. (4) the mandate of Government Departments or agencies. (5) the budgets for promotion of publications and films. (6) the mechanisms for consultation between the Government and the private sector. He will also prepare a dossier of relevant statistics and Government statements for subsequent analysis by the Secretary of State's Department, (b) $5,000 plus $1,000 accountable travel expenses.
2.	Emphasis will be placed on those European countries which have problems comparable to those of Canada i.e. countries of a bilingual or multilingual nature, countries of small population, countries with larger neighbours of the same language, etc. The contract commenced on March 1, 1976 and ends on October 29, 1976.
3.	To the knowledge of the Secretary of State Department no such research work as it pertains to Canada has been carried out since the O'Leary Report "Canada Royal Commission on Publications 1961".

speechtext: Has the government or its agencies taken, in the last six months, any action to make members of the Canadian Armed Forces, formerly resident in Atlantic Canada, eligible to compete in closed competitions held by the Public Service in the Atlantic provinces without regard for the geographical or organizational limits prescribed by the competition and, if so, what was such action?

speakeroldname: Miss Coline Campbell (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
maintopic: ELIGIBILITY OF FORMER MEMBERS OF CANADIAN ARMED
subtopic: FORCES IN PSC COMPETITIONS IN ATLANTIC PROVINCES
speechtext: I am informed by the Public Service Commission as follows: No. The commission, under the provision of Section 13(b) of the Public Service Employment Act, is required to consider only the part of the public service and the occupational nature and level of positions in which prospective candidates must be employed at the time the closed competition is held, in order to be eligible for appointment. Therefore, former residence in a geographical area does not make a candidate eligible to compete in competitions open only to people occupying positions in that same geographical area. In the last six months, the commission has taken no action to change this requirement.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have felt somewhat like Alice in Wonderland these past few weeks, listening to the debates in the House of Commons. The cry has been "Off with his head", as if that would magically solve our problems. Such a simple solution, so cavalier!
This is an awesome responsibility that we face, Mr. Speaker, and we have a duty to think things through for ourselves. You may remember, in the play "Caesar and Cleopatra," that Caesar says:
To the end of history, murder shall breed murder, always in the name of right and honour and peace, until the gods are tired of blood, and create a race that can understand.
Understanding is the key. Murder does breed murder, and violence does breed violence. These people on death row are the product of our society; and if these people have failed, our society in a measure has failed as well. Therefore, we must examine our society and discover the circumstances that led people to commit mdrder and other crimes, and then let us try to eliminate the causes.
I do not think we can set ourselves up to judge our fellow man so harshly that we say to anyone that they are not fit to live. If we condemn these people to death, we are telling them that there is no hope for them in this world. And who are we to take away hope? When we take away hope for them, we take away the sense of hope for us all. How do we know but that through some ironic twist of circumstance we ourselves could end up on death row, as could someone we know or love? How truly awful to be told that there is no hope for them, that they are beyond redemption. I think we had better not be too self-righteous
[Mr. Roy (Laval).l
and complacent. I think we should remind ourselves that "There but for the grace of God, go I".
I am pleased to note that all the major churches and religions are in favour of abolition of the death penalty, as are the criminologists and humanitarians. While these people may not form the majority opinion, they can take comfort from something Adlai Stevenson once said. He said that all progress has resulted from people who took unpopular positions.
As for this entire question of public opinion, it can be easily manipulated by the media and by pressure groups. We who have the personal responsibility to vote on the hanging bill cannot in conscience, simply rely on the latest poll to make our decision for us. When I sent out my own questionnaire in Burnaby-Seymour on the issue of capital punishment, only 4 per cent of the people answered the survey, most of them favouring capital punishment. One could also note that 96 per cent of the people of that riding left the decision to me. Meanwhile, the government is bringing in Bill C-83, which will introduce stronger measures to protect society.
There are those who believe capital punishment is a deterrent. According to the statistics, it is not. The lowest murder rates in the world are found in countries where capital punishment has been abolished: for example, Sweden, and in the American states of Minnesota, Wisconsin, Rhode Island and Maine. On the other hand, some of the highest murder rates are found where capital punishment is, or was, in force until recently: for instance, in France, Spain, Florida, Georgia, South Carolina and Louisiana.
The unhappy statistics of murder also disclose that most killings are the result of domestic quarrels or love triangles, crimes of passion. In Canada, for example, in a 13-year period ending in 1974 there were 4,500 murders and only 559 took place during the commission of a criminal act.
Given, then, the sudden, unplanned nature of most homicides, it appears highly unlikely that most people who commit murder take into account the threat of capital punishment before carrying out that act. In the case of criminals, they know full well that the police carry weapons, and even the danger of on-the-spot capital punishment does not serve as a deterrent. As for the argument that the cost of keeping prisoners is a financial burden to the taxpayers, I find that a ridiculous and cynical argument. One might as well argue against the high cost of trials and appeals. This argument also ignores the fact that inmates do work in prison and are paid wages lower than scale.
I believe that instead of wasting time and dwelling on this gruesome subject, debating whether or not we are going to hang those few people who are already sweating it out on death row, we should busy ourselves with examining our society and improving it. We must ask these questions of ourselves: What is there in our society that drives people to violence? Our figures show that most murders are domestic. It is probably true that, as Thoreau said, "Most men live lives of quiet desperation", but why is that so? Is it too difficult in our society today to raise a happy family? Is it too difficult in this affluent country just to
May 25, 1976

make a living? Are we goaded beyond our means by the commercialism of our age? Are we teased into wanting too much? Has the crassness of the market place already placed necessities beyond the reach of many people?
Many people today are concerned about the violence, the negativism and the crime depicted in the media. I wonder, too, where are the stories of real heroes that might inspire us to new heights of achievement, such as George Washington Carver, Florence Nightingale, Wilberforce, John Stuart Mill, Mahatma Gandhi, Einstein and Schweitzer? Where are the best from other countries? We have had so much blather in the media about capital punishment and the grisly details of crime that one wonders where is the emphasis on the art of living. As Carl Jung wrote, "The art of living is the rarest and most distinguished of all the arts . . . Whoeyer succeeded in draining the whole cup with grace?"
Our aim should be an ideal society. You may remember Schiller writing "Only the ideal can bring humans to unity. And the ideal has as its foundation ... knowledge". We must have the courage and honesty to look at our society critically and see where it is wanting. We could look to the happy, healthy societies in the world and see how they are achieving this. We could ask ourselves, what are our goals?
I hope this parliament, in a free vote, will vote with hope, with mercy and with confidence that we can abolish forever the barbaric custom of capital punishment. Surely, in this space age, when we have landed men on the moon and have seen miracles in so many fields of human endeavour, we do not have to retain such a medieval practice. I think it has no place in a civilized society.
As a matter of interest, I want to quote something Eugene Debs once said to a judge:
Your Honour, years ago I recognized my kinship with all living beings . . . and I made up my mind that I was not one bit better than the meanest of the earth. I said then and I say now ... that while there is a lower class, I am in it... while there is a criminal element, I am of it.. . while there is a soul in prison, I am not free-
For more than ten years parliament has been poised on the edge of full abolition. Once again the House of Commons has the opportunity to abolish a practice which deprives society of any means to rectify its mistakes; a practice which is abhorrent and which adds the suffering of innocent family members to that of the guilty.
I suggest we vote on this bill with hope for life, not hopelessness with death. I suggest we vote with confidence that we can look critically at our society and see where it is wanting and, hopefully, find our way in changing that society. If our society is indeed leading to crime, there is something very wrong with it. For our own good we must come to grips with the problem. The answer does not lie in hanging a few people to show how tough we are. Unless we come to grips honestly with the problem, I fear that, as Caesar says in the play:
To the end of history, murder shall breed murder ... always in the name of right and honour and peace, until the gods are tired of blood, and create a race that can understand.
Thank you, Mr. Speaker.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to begin by saying that my remarks during this very
Capital Punishment
important debate will outline essentially my own personal views. I do, however, acknowledge with deep appreciation and thanks the heavy volume of mail I have received on the combined issue of capital punishment and peace and security. I have received the heaviest mail ever in my 3Vi years in this House on these two issues.
During the current debate, about 350 individuals have let me know about their feelings on this combined issue, and none of this group is from outside my own constituency of Medicine Hat. These constituency views were contained mostly in personal letters and unsolicited petitions. I did not conduct any formal or informal poll or survey as I did on the previous capital punishment debate in 1973. I freely acknowledge that the greater number of letters dealt with the companion bill on peace and security, Bill C-83. I say this now because I was one of approximately 27 members of this House who was unable to participate in that debate because of the government's closure action.
The ratio in support of the retention of capital punishment in my constituency mail was 17 to 1. After reviewing all these constituency letters, I have decided that in addition to some very blunt comments about the specific issue, there is another, deeper and more serious message-between the lines, if you like; but it is there and it cannot be ignored. That message is one of widespread concern over the state of our nation's apparent attitudes pertaining to law and order. There is deep concern that our respect for law and order and morality has sunk to an all-time low.
These letters make it very clear that the underlying reason for a resurgence in the call for capital punishment is this deep concern over law and order in Canada today. Out of sheer desperation and concern, Canadians are saying that something must be done, that nothing has been done by this government to recognize and abate this obvious trend to national lawlessness, and a growing philosophy in the belief that maybe-just maybe-crime does pay.
Whether we agree that capital punishment can be a meaningful deterrent, my constituents are saying that until something better comes along as a deterrent, we had better bring back, in fact, capital punishment. To those of you who say that the necessary deterrence essential for proper law and order will be provided by this bill and its companion, Bill C-83, I say, very simply, it is three years too late. This government had the opportunity to do something at the time of the last capital punishment debate three years ago with respect to meaningful deterrence. The signs of social concern were plainly evident then, although not as pronounced as now. I was personally concerned about those signs and spoke of them in my first election campaign in 1972. The government's stand-pat attitude in 1973 has been an open invitation to increased crime and violence ever since.
What I have been saying was also expressed much more eloquently by my hon. colleague from Edmonton-Strath-cona (Mr. Roche) in his very thought-provoking speech in this debate as recorded on page 13219 of Hansard for May 5. I commend it to all members of this House and, indeed, to all Canadians at this time. He was so right when he pointed out that "Canada is not yet ready for total abolition" because the current climate for total abolition is

Capital Punishment
wrong. We should read again and again his statement as follows:
I cannot isolate the principle of abolition from real conditions in our country. The reality is that it is better to keep capital punishment in limited cases than to rush total abolition and diminish respect for the law... And even be prepared to preserve an inferior type of law if necessary.
There is deep concern and infuriation over the package concept of these companion bills on peace and security and capital punishment. The good features of Bill C-83, and there are certainly some, are being deliberately overlooked because of the feeling we are being bribed and coerced into accepting the total package. Suffice it to say that the two bills that make up this package amend old legislation and mix new legislation with it, in the package concept-a situation that simply invites controversy both in our debates in the House and especially at the committee stage.
Also, part of that package is the new use of the term "free vote" in this House. It is difficult to understand the rationale of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) in their repeated statements that our vote on this bill will be a free vote but that the cabinet will support the bill. For sheer double-talk and hypocrisy we should read again the Prime Minister's response to his own party member from Vancouver-Kings-way when she asked: "Will the free vote on Bill C-84 be free to the cabinet?" The Prime Minister's response was: "Mr. Speaker, a freer group of men and women still has to be found in Canada".
The rationale behind this free vote approach must surely relate to the fact that cabinet has been breaking the law every time it fails to carry out a court's decision calling for capital punishment by abusing its prerogative to grant commutation and is now taking the expedient course of changing the law that still has another year to run. Of course, this change is to be made well before the 1978 election, in the hope that the public will have forgotten these manipulations by then. I acknowledged at the beginning of these comments that my constituency mail on this issue has been very enlightening and rewarding to me, personally. In order to illustrate these "messages between the lines" in these letters from home, I would like to quote a few succinct phrases and statements from some of the mail. From Medicine Hat:
Our governments, federally and provincially, have been handing out lollipops to criminals convicted of major crimes and are now reaping the harvest.
From a rural clergyman in southern Alberta:
The government seems to be relying excessively on prisons, more and more of them. If hanging be not a deterrent, neither is imprisonment. Our prison system is almost universally acknowledged a failure and yet we are rapidly expanding it... The whole approach is topsy-turvy. It is like combating lung cancer by doing nothing except removing diseased lungs. How much better it is to get people not to smoke. It may be difficult to persuade them, and some will not listen, but the effort must be made. The federal government seems to do very little to persuade people to avoid contracting the cancer of crime.
From Cardston, Alberta:
Omnibus bills are a tool of government whereby members may be pressured into supporting "package" legislation, almost inevitably compromising their position on at least part of the package.

From Bow Island, Alberta:
Further, I would urge that all people receiving a jail sentence should be required to produce or work to pay for the expenses incurred.
From Turin, Alberta:
An honest man has nothing to fear about capital punishment.
As a layman in matters relating to religion, but as one who considers himself a practical Christian, firmly believing in the moral and spiritual rights of each of us as individuals, I continue to be amazed, and indeed sometimes confused, about two features of this aspect of the debate. First, the frequent and very genuine references to the Bible in support of either side of this emotional debate. There are literally dozens of quotes available for this purpose. Most of the retentionist quotes are from the Old Testament, while the abolitionist support is from the New Testament. Second, I have the feeling that most abolitionists seem to assume that we retentionists cannot possibly be following the exercise of our personal conscience, whereas abolitionists are truly following their own personal conscience.
I know I will have to disagree with many of my close personal friends, and even relatives, on this issue. While I am pleased, and even obligated, to hear the views of all my constituents where possible, I do not in any way attempt to persuade others to agree with me. I have been known to try to convince others of my viewpoint on other issues, such as our national beef cattle situation, or our local Suffield issue in Medicine Hat-but not on this one. My personal decision on this capital punishment bill will be the most serious, soul-searching decision I have ever been called on to make as a member of this House.
Before leaving this portion of my comments, it seems appropriate to express the feeling that surely it is time for the CBC to cease using that background picture of the hangman's noose on the national TV news when a government news item appears on capital punishment. I am certain I have support for this from other members. I certainly have it from my constituents' letters. Of the many references that all members of parliament have received, I wish to quote briefly from only two. The first is from the Pentecostal Assemblies of Canada, with reference to the Solicitor General's view on deterrence:
What the Solicitor General says may be true of some irrational people. But we believe that capital punishment by due process of law, for calculated premeditated murder by any rational person, does have a deterrent.
There is a further quotation from the Pentecostal group:
We believe also, in principle, that the use of executive clemency by governor in council was a bad practice because, in effect, it made the cabinet rehear the case, and for all practical purposes, constitute another court.
The second author I wish to quote is Dr. Fattah, from Simon Fraser University, who predicts the practical results that could follow the implementation of Bill C-84 if the bill passes. I will paraphrase his suggestions. He states that, first, a considerable number of cases of first-degree murder will be reduced to second-degree. Second, acquittal rates in cases of first-degree murder will be very high, and third, a large number of first-degree murder cases will end with the jury handing out a verdict of not guilty by reason of
May 25, 1976

insanity. Finally, I should like to quote the following statement of Dr. Fattah:
I still remember back in January of 1973, when Marcel Prud'homme, MP for Montreal, Saint-Denis, and James Fleming, MP for York West, suggested that the government bill be amended to imprison killers for a minimum of 25 years. Solicitor General Allmand and other members of the cabinet were the first to declare their opposition. It is disconcerting and disenchanting to see the government, after only three years, adopt the same retrogressive suggestion it once condemned.
I can only add that I can certainly associate myself with these appropriate quotations. In my opening comments I made reference to our concern for the lack of respect for law and order in our society today. Those of us in the Medicine Hat-Redcliff community, including the immediate rural area, have a very special reason to be concerned.
I want to refer very briefly to a terrible tragedy that occurred on August 22, 1974, when a young, 17-year old service station employee was brutally murdered while on duty during the late night hours. Three young hitchhikers robbed the service station of $123.60 and in the process murdered the young attendant by using a mechanic's hammer in a brutal fashion. No firearms were used, but drugs and alcohol were definitely involved. Two of the three young criminals were also involved in an earlier murder in the St. Catharines area that had been committed prior to the Medicine Hat tragedy. Again, no firearms were involved.
I am sure that our Medicine Hat citizens are still asking themselves, "Do we need to have tragedies like this to establish the need for comprehensive and practical law and order guidelines?" As Canadians we have become overly complacent about crime, especially so-called petty crimes. Why should we have to have almost nightly break-ins and robberies in a small city such as Medicine Hat, sometimes as many as eight or ten in a single night? It has been suggested that perhaps many of us no longer believe in evil, only in error or accident. Why are most, if not all, of the current polls so heavily in favour of the retention of capital punishment? Surely it has to be because of this very state of lawlessness in our Canadian society about which I am so concerned.
I should like to conclude by drawing the attention of the House to the sentiments expressed by my colleague, the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens), when he received one of the biggest responses for a one-liner at our recent leadership convention, which is as follows:
Imagine a Canada in which justice reflects the realities of the public will. Whose rights need the greater protection, the criminals' or their victims?
The rights of the victims of crime must be paramount in our system.
In the final analysis, Mr. Speaker, I cannot support this bill to abolish capital punishment in Canada.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, thank you for the opportunity this afternoon to speak in this debate. The issue being debated this afternoon is more involved than the isolated decision to retain or to abolish capital punishment. Canada still has to face a whole complex of questions about the reform of corrections, parole and rehabilitation. The bill that is now before us in parliament to extend the suspension of the death penalty treats, in an isolated way, a problem which is connected with these many other problems.
Capital Punishment
I come from an almost completely God-loving community; I have listened to and read what my constituents have to say, and I think that they have said many things. But, most importantly, they have in some way repeated what has been stated by many of our church authorities. I would like to convey to you the statement of Bishop W. E. Power, president of the Canadian Catholic Conference, who says:
We consider it an illegitimate use of the Bible, especially the Old Testament, to quote texts in order to argue, in our time, for the retention of the death penalty. Each biblical text supporting the death penalty must be studied in the light of its historical context, and not simply applied to present-day Canada. Furthermore, each such Old Testament text must be weighed against many passages in the New Testament where Jesus constantly rejects the normal human tendency to redress injury by injury and calls instead for generosity. He established the norm that violence and hostility are not corrected by countermeasures of violence and hostility.
I have listened to many hon. members, both the reten-tionists and abolitionists, and I am convinced that nothing new has been said to change my mind in any way. The question of the death penalty ought not to focus on whether a convicted murderer, no matter how wanton, deserves to die. The focus should be on us: Should Canadians, as a community, try to break the escalating spiral of violence by refraining from violence, the same violence that some profess will serve as a deterrent? The Canadian Catholic Conference goes on to say:
To a Christian, whose starting point is reverence for the sanctity of life, the death penalty can surely be only a desperate resort. A Christian must be utterly convinced of its social necessity before supporting it. Our society, it is true, has traditionally exacted the death penalty. But this ought not to mean, as it often seems, that those who favour suspension must bear the burden of proof. On the contrary, those who favour retention should be required to convince a Christian of its necessity.
I would hope, Mr. Speaker, along with many others, that we would investigate further and establish research committees to make an exhaustive study of all the ramifications of this complex problem and then publish these reports within a specified period. As one who three weeks after he was elected witnessed a murder, a shooting of three innocent people, and as one who held the body of the murdered man in his arms, I realized that I was a firm believer in the reverence and the sanctity of life.
I am rather inclined to agree with our Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) who said that capital punishment is not only ineffective but also immoral, and who listed the following alternatives which I feel are worth repeating here. There should be better trained, better deployed and better equipped policemen; effective gun control; proactive, rather than reactive, police work; more effective correctional programs for juveniles and adults; more effective social and economic programs to remove the causes of crime; improved treatment for alcoholics and drug addicts; improved education and recreation programs; possible restrictions on the showing of violence on television and through other media; and measures to promote respect for legitimate authority in the home, the school, the church, community associations, and government.
I think we had better return to family life basics and to the great respect which some of our ethnic communities demonstrate toward family life and toward the reverence

for the sanctity of life. I think we must return to the three "R's-Reverence, Respect" and, most importantly, the "Right to Life."
Thank you, Mr. Speaker, for the opportunity to participate in this very profound debate. I am inclined to agree with our Solicitor General and our government that if these and other measures I have mentioned were pursued with more vigour, we would do much more to lower our crime rate than if we merely emphasized the application of harsh penalties after the fact.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to point out to the House that this is a completely needless debate. There is legislation on the statute books at this very moment which will not expire for another three or four years. I can see no reason whatever for having this debate today. An experiment is in progress. When we voted the last time, we were told that an experiment was to take place. The government has prejudged the outcome of this experiment and has decided, in its own wisdom, that the experiment was a failure, and we are being asked to write off the experiment and abolish the death penalty. This is a needless debate. Never in my life have I seen anything more needless than this particular piece of legislation.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: Why speak on it, then?

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: I am speaking on it because it needs to be drawn to the attention of the public that it is needless. It is a diversion to take the minds of the public off the serious things which are going on in this country and the failure of this government to deal with our economic problems.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
How can this government trot out data and conclusions, which is done through the auspices of a pet professor of the government by the name of Fattah, to prove that the experiment has been a failure? It is presumptuous on the part of the government, and on top of that, it is very unscientific. Therefore, I conclude that this is a needless debate. It is diversionary, bearing in mind the legislation which is already on the books, and it is meant to draw attention away from the economic ills which beset this country and to lull those who are really concerned about the failure of law and order in this country, for which this government must take a very large responsibility, and particularly those who are living alone on fixed incomes and who are worried about the economic problems. It is a complete fraud.
It is a cynical misuse of the time of this House to suggest that we must approve this bill before we are allowed out of this House at the end of next month. Are we going to accept that sort of blackmail? That is what it is. There is legislation on the books now. Why should we be subjected to blackmail at this particular time? Why now? Why the rush? Why this bill?
Not for one minute do I believe that this government, which is bringing forward this needless legislation and trying to rush it through, is motivated in this effort by any of the stirrings of philosophic concern for human beings. The motivations of this government are entirely cynical in

this as in many other of its activities. Why now? Why the rush? Why do we have to pass this bill before the end of June, when there is legislation already on the books? It is just to obscure the economic problems besetting this country. It is just to obfuscate.
If there were any true and purely philosophical motivations, why should the government not be concerned about the law-abiding and those who respect the law, rather than pretending that it is moved by the poor, unfortunate, misguided criminal?
If such, indeed, is the motivation of the government, why does it delay so long in sorting out the good from the bad; the recoverable from those who cannot be rehabilitated amongst inmates? This is where the problem lies. This is where the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) should be directing his attention-not to wasting the time of this House on needless legislation such as the legislation he has brought forward. Why allow the prisoners in this country to convert prisons into post-graduate institutions where inmates can be instructed on how to beat the law? That is what our prisons have been turned into. Prisoners learn how to pick locks, how to make ice picks and how to hold hostages. Young offenders, through some error, have landed up in some of our penal institutions and are being faced with this sort of deadbeat, the inmate who cannot be rehabilitated. Once the young offender has lapsed once and gets into the hands of those old cons, he is finished; he becomes a criminal for life. This is where rehabilitation should take place.
This bill is not only a needless bit of legislation, but it is bad, bad, and I intend to vote against it. There are certain special aspects to this legislation, however, with which I would like to deal. I could start on page 1 of the bill and go through it seriatim, page by page, but I am going to confine myself to two or three aspects. I would like to deal with the proposal of this government to remove treason as one of the crimes punishable by death. The Encyclopedia Bri-tannica talks of treason in this way:
The law which punishes treason is a necessary consequence of the idea of a state and is essential to the existence of the state.
If there is no law protecting the state against treason, I submit our state is in trouble. In Roman law, the crime of treason was next in gravity to sacrilege, and if it was so serious, and if it is so serious-and I think it is-should it not be punishable by the ultimate penalty? Since by custom and tradition cases of treason are justiciable by special processes, the seriousness of the felony is amply marked. It is a serious crime, and in clause 2 the government proposes to dispose of it and consider that anyone who has committed treason will be subject to life imprisonment rather than the ultimate penalty.
I find it inexplicable that the government should seek to eliminate the death penalty for treason, whether it be against a head of state, a monarch, a sovereign or the forcible overthrow of government. If there is no deterrent to forestall treasonable acts-that is, attacks on our institutions with the object of destroying them-then what motivation is there to make us want to defend those institutions? This is the problem that this government has not faced.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Surely these concepts mirror one another: the existence of one determining the existence of the other, just as the absence of a deterrent predetermines the absence of motivation. If I do not hold dear my democratic institutions, be they persons or functional organizations, such as the one in which I proudly speak today and condemn to the ultimate penalty anyone who ventures to deprive me of them, how can I be expected to defend those same institutions with my life, as many of us in this House did 30 and more years ago?
What sort of mentality can draft such legislation? Perhaps I should ask: What sort of mentality can insist that such legislation be drafted? I am not blaming the drafters, but those who instruct the drafters to put this sort of legislation before us. Is no one on that side of the House who supports this bill prepared to defend with his life those very institutions in which we are permitted to discuss this matter freely and openly? Well, I am. Is everyone prepared to tolerate the violent overthrow of those institutions without lifting a finger? Well, I'm not. The death penalty should certainly be imposed upon those who commit treason against the head of state, against those who wage war against this country or assist others in doing so, or who use force-

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: -to overthrow the government, or who commit any other of the incidental treasonable acts outlined in sections 46 and 47 of the Criminal Code. If we remove that ultimate penalty, Mr. Speaker, we will have filleted our nation-we will have removed its backbone and removed from our citizens the will to stand up and defend our way of life when it is threatened. Is that what this government wants? I sometimes think they do.

I sometimes wonder whether members on the other side have even read this bill. They have been talking about the noose and all that sort of stuff that gets people worked up emotionally. Clause 3 is equally wrong-piracy, presumably including the hijacking of people and aircraft. Where there is loss of life, the punishment would be life imprisonment. Section 214 of the Criminal Code is the focus of much attention in the present debate. It concerns the penalty for killing a policeman or prison guard. Leave it for those cases to which it now applies and for the additional ones suggested, because some people attempting to break out or to create a disturbance may not be in prison for the crime of first-degree murder. I would prefer to see sections 218(1) to (4) remain on the statute books as they are. They should not be considered as experimental provisions but as formal points of our law.
I have not dealt with the other proposed sections which redefine murder as first and second-degree murder; one of those offences would be punishable by a long sentence of imprisonment, with provision for parole after a certain period of sentence has elapsed. I suggest, as I suggested at the beginning, that this legislation is wrong. It is diversionary. There is no need for it at present. We are being asked to spend time considering this legislation rather than considering important economic questions which confront our elderly and those on fixed incomes. By acting in this fashion, the government is being dishonest with parliament and the Canadian people.
I propose to stand up when the time comes and vote against the bill. As far as I am concerned, the time need not come before the end of June. The bill could be voted on at any time in the next three years. There is no need at all to vote on the bill now.

Mr. Speaker, may I say at the beginning of my remarks, concerning capital punishment that I respect the opinion of those supporting the bill.
My comments will be very brief. The society has rights, for instance the right to protect itself against those willing to destroy it or destroy some individuals who are part of it. I would like to stress that I used the word "protect" and
May 25, 1976

not "revenge". In this bill, I see nothing indicating convincingly that by abolishing capital punishment we could, with the sentence increased to 25 years of imprisonment, prevent some individuals from committing one or several murders. On the contrary, extending the penalty to 25 years' imprisonment clearly indicates that the offence must be related to the punishment, in the minds of those who have drafted this legislation.
Many references have been made to rehabilitation during this debate especially in relation to crime offenders. I would like to emphasize, Mr. Speaker, that as long as all segments of our society do not feel protected by a just and fair law, there cannot be rehabilitation. This means changes in our social structure, better administration of justice, specialized prevention training for police forces and jail wardens, a review of parole and a rehabilitation plan for those who can still be reclaimed. I must also mention a compensation plan for victims, a review of appeal procedure against the death sentence, whenever the jury has recommended leniency. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the final ruling should be heard, not in the way it is done in Cabinet, but before three Supreme Court justices.
I would like to point out that the best way to reduce crime and have an adequate penal system is certainly to increase the opportunity for the guilty party to be brought to court and sentenced to a penalty which includes capital punishment for premeditated murder. For those reasons, Mr. Speaker, having stated I would be brief, I shall only repeat very clearly that I intend to vote against this bill, that is for the retention of capital punishment for premeditated murder.
