subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the subject matter of the bill before us was considered in 1961, 1966, 1967, and 1973. Each time it was lengthily and strongly debated, and those who participated expressed contradictory opinions and, until now, we are continuing the same experience because the matter is very controversial.
At any stage of the voting, each member will have to take his responsibilities, for this is a free vote, whatever may think some members of the official opposition. Such particularity implies that the member has an individual role to play and that the line of the party gives way to the voice of the conscience and to the constituents' interest, that is to say that the member votes according to his own assessment of the matter.
First, it is important to place the debate in its general contemporary context. We must above all forget the out-ofdate concepts of the death penalty and consider the problem in the light of present perspectives. First of all, it is essential to abandon the ancient law of retaliation, retribution of an eye for an eye through vengeful punishment.
Ideas, customs and needs of the criminal policy have been changing with time. The problem must therefore be approached in a state of mind adapted to the circumstances of our times. It is not useless, therefore, to recall that Canadian criminal law has made substantial progress in this regard. Is there need to point out some effects of the 1961 act in this field? Since that time, capital punishment has been eliminated for many categories of murders, and
Capital Punishment
remains applicable only in the case of qualified murder, and even then the jury may recommend clemency or leniency if they feel this is warranted by the circumstances. Moreover, the 1961 legislation provides for an automatic revision of the case by an appeal court, particularly with regard to questions of law, propriety of procedure and facts. The convicted person is thus given the right to appeal to the Supreme Court. Whether the murderer is rich or poor, his or her case can thus be brought before the highest tribunal in the land without prior authorization. Finally, since 1961, no person under 18 can be given a death sentence. It can therefore be said that in this field, Canadian criminal law has become more humane and that the death penalty is practically brought upon particularly odious criminals only.
Our conception of this punishment and its finality has obviously changed. It is now out of question to impose punishment on the criminal without caring about his rehabilitation merely to set a terrifying example for the citizens. Whatever opinion we have on that subject, we all agree that we should render an offender harmless through reform. Everytime it is possible and not through sheer suppression, everytime circumstances allow it, we must try to rehabilitate the criminal and bring back a social being who can live and be a useful member in society. Having said that, there certainly are convicted criminals who cannot be amended, rehabilitated or socially recuperated and who will finally remain a danger for the community.
It is under that aspect of danger and real necessity that capital punishment must be considered, that is to eliminate once and for all a deadly risk. Capital punishment nowadays should not be considered as a "vindictive torture" but as a "means of defence", an ultimate means to protect the society. It is therefore a matter of social protection by preventing killing and, if necessary, by eliminating beings who are essentially antisocial and a permanent risk for the community. Those who favour abolition of capital punishment put forward various arguments but I want to consider only a few of them.
First, some abolitionists question the state's right to take the life of a citizen. For sure, this debate concerns not only the political concept one may have of the state, but also the religious convictions of every individual. Without starting a philosophical debate, let us say that in Canada nothing takes away such a power from the federal government. Under the constitution, criminal law comes under federal jurisdiction and, furthermore, pursuant to section 91 of the British North America Act, Parliament has the necessary authority to make laws for the maintenance of peace, order and good government of Canada. Thus, the government has not only the power but also the duty to protect the common good and, to that end, it must take all the necessary steps to ensure the security of all citizens and to protect the lives of innocent people.
When the problem is viewed from the angle of the protection of society and the defence of the community, it seems hardly possible to question the right of the state to eliminate dangerous and hopeless individuals once and for all. When dealing with some particularly infamous criminal, does the state not have the right to resort to any measure, if necessary, to the most drastic, in order to protect the rest of society, particularly prison staff and

May 25, 1976
Capital Punishment
other inmates? It is also to spare the lives of prison staff, of citizens in general, and possibly of some members of the community in case of an invasion, for example, that the state must, in certain cases, eliminate the individual who is a threat to society. Is it not also under this duty that the state must protect the common good and ensure the security of the country by declaring war at times?
How can we challenge the state's right to take the life of a dangerous criminal when it has the right to demand from the citizens any sacrifice necessary for the protection of society and the defence of the country? The state can compel soldiers to give their lives for the safety of the country. So why could it not, in order to attain an end of the same order, resort to the death penalty? In some cases, the duty to take the life of an individual is no more unethical than the duty to kill in times of war or in cases of self-defence. By the way, the death penalty is the selfdefence of society and the protection of its members. Even the Canadian Catholic Conference, that is the Assembly of Catholic Bishops of Canada, in a recent release, in recommending the abolition of capital punishment on humane grounds, recognized the state certain rights in this area, and I quote:
This stand taken by the bishops does not deny the state the right to impose capital punishment if circumstances were to demand it, nor is it intended to bind every Christian in his personal opinion on this subject.
Here is what His Holiness Pope Pius XXII stated in 1952 with respect to the rights of the state in the matter of capital punishment, and I quote:
It is the prerogative of the political power to deprive the convict of the blessing of life in atonement for his sin, when, through his crime, he lost the right to live.
Second, some abolitionists believe that capital punishment does not deter anyone from committing a crime or has hardly a deterrent effect on him, and that life imprisonment is equally effective. In our society, Mr. Speaker, opinions are divided on the deterrent effect of capital punishment on murderers. I do not think one can use statistics in support of an argument. Statistics are subject to various interpretations and are uncertain. It is nearly impossible to make a useful comparison between countries because of the differences in the legal definition of crimes, legal procedures and court practices, methods used to compile crime statistics, morality standards, and finally political and economical and social conditions. Those are data that defy any valid assessment.
Strict enforcement of the death penalty certainly does not prevent the perpetration of all deliberate murders. In fact, murderers rely on their guile to escape either the police or a conviction for lack of sufficient evidence. Hence, the care they take to escape pursuit. Caught in the act they shoot down the policemen who want to arrest them. In the expectation of criminal prosecution, they do not hesitate in some cases to murder witnesses who would lead to their conviction. This is an indication of the terrible fear they have of capital punishment. As a matter of fact, all punishments are exemplary. We do not park our car in a no-parking zone because we fear getting a ticket. If all punishments are designed to intimidate the offender-and they do have this result to a large extent-how in Heavens

would capital punishment, the harshest of all, miss its goal?
It is perhaps difficult to establish the relationship between capital punishment and crime. However, obviously the concept of this extreme retribution remains closely related to that of some barbarous and abominable crimes. This severeness of punishment concept has undoubtedly been deep rooted in people's mind for generations, and commonsense dictates that no threat other than that of losing one's life would deter a potential criminal from perpetrating a murder.
Moreover, the Senate and House of Commons Joint Committee on Capital Punishment stated in its 1956 report, and I quote:
The law enforcement authorities consider that capital punishment is an effective deterrent to crime, particularly as it prevents professional criminals from using guns and committing violent offences. Capital punishment protects the police forces in so far as a criminal who wants to escape arrest would fear to a lesser extent the consequences of using firearms or resorting to violence if capital punishment did not exist.
Certainly you will be told that this did not prevent policemen and prison guards from being murdered.
Mr. Speaker, capital punishment no longer exists in Canada since 1962, when a death sentence was executed for the last time in this country. Since the current law on capital punishment went into force, 36 police officers and prison guards were killed. Every death sentence for capital murder has been commuted to life imprisonment by the Cabinet. This in certain cases means less than 15 years imprisonment or waiting for Parliament to decide on this legislation.
The third point I would like to make concerns the danger that an innocent be executed following a judicial errror. This is a possibility, but how very remote and problematical. Very few convincing cases can be referred to, because the fact that someone admits to commiting a crime for which someone else has been punished is not sufficient proof that the latter was innocent.
On the possibility of error, on June 27, 1956, the Commons and Senate Joint Committee on Capital Punishment had this to say, as appears on page 60, paragraph 60, of the White Paper on Capital Punishment, and I quote:
Considerable emphasis was put on the risk of irrevocable error in capital convictions. The fact that there was no known Canadian instance of the execution of an innocent person indicated the effectiveness of present procedures by way of trial and executive review and this suggests that the risk of error does not present a reasonable argument for abolition in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, since that report was published, there has been a reinforcement of safeguards against possible execution of innocent people, through Criminal Code and judicial procedure reforms, which practically eliminated any possibility of an error on facts. The death sentence is not given on simple circumstantial evidence any more. Appeal is mandatory up to and including the Supreme Court, which allows the higher courts to review every case and find any minor flow in the Crown's evidence. Then must follow an exhaustive review by the Solicitor General and finally by the Cabinet, and the Cabinet can always use its right to commute a death penalty. It is evident that in all those phases, the least doubt must necessarily be considered in favour of the accused. We already exempt from the death penalty those who kill in a fit of passion, jeal-
May 25, 1976

ousy or anger. We give special consideration in certain cases, for instance a man who is overly nervous and mortally wounds the police officer who tries to capture him.
Mr. Speaker, when the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) pointed out that in 1966 there was a miscarriage of justice, he mentioned the United States and England but could not refer to a single case in Canada. Mr. Speaker, the present act has been in force since December 29, 1967 and in 1973 it was extended for another five year period for several reasons, particularly, that a longer period would give the authorities better statistical data.
Now the government has introduced in Parliament Bill C-84 to amend the Criminal Code as regards murder and certain other serious offences, which would replace capital punishment for premeditated murder by life imprisonment. That means in certain cases 25 years imprisonment, but in other cases, after having served 15 years, after being convicted, the inmate could file an application to serve less time before being eligible for parole. I remember that in 1973 an amendment was presented to replace capital punishment by 25 years imprisonment. Mr. Speaker, as concerns such an amendment, members of Parliament, association spokesmen and individuals told us that emprisonment for such a long period is more inhuman than capital punishment itself. To further support this argument, I would like to quote a few excerpts from various newspapers following the announcement of the new peace and security legislation.
On February 25, 1976, the Montreal Start published an editorial which read, and I quote:
By filling up prisons with men sentenced to endless penalties, we are sure to transform these men in time-bombs and to expose prison personnel to a terrible danger.
Mr. Normand Caron, general director of the Human Rights League, stated, and I quote from the newspaper La Presse of February 26, 1976:
These new amendments can only lead to even more desperate people who will not hesitate to attempt an escape faced with a hopeless future.
On the same day and in the same newspaper, the Association of Social Workers gave the following warning in a press release:
We realize that the public must be better protected against criminals, but we do not believe that longer prison sentences are the answer to this problem. In fact, we have every reason to believe that such sentences would only make the problem worse.
Mr. Speaker, while recognizing that many people would like capital punishment to disappear, even more people support and accept it. This support reflects the aversion of the public for murder, the worst of crimes. Moreover, we recognize that public hatred for murder reflects a traditional attitude resulting from the fact that the death penalty is reserved for this crime in particular.
The abolition of the penalty considered traditionally as a fair and effective deterrent could only be recommended if there was clear evidence that the ordinary citizen believes this penalty to be clearly ineffective. The experience of the authorities shows that abolition of the death penalty when the public strongly favours its retention can cause confusion and doubt, which can have disastrous effects on the administration of justice.
Capital Punishment
Mr. Speaker, I said in 1973 and I repeat it with more emphasis today that at a time when the state has much to do to control crime, we should be more concerned about protecting society rather than the criminal. There are reasons to believe that the death penalty is a deterrent against armed robbery and the abolition of the death penalty could be interpreted by those who disregard the law as a signal to commit other criminal acts.
At the beginning of my comments, Mr. Speaker, I said that each member should make his own decision, since it is a free vote. This is why I for one cannot support this legislation because I am absolutely convinced that the fear of a violent death has an intimidating effect and is the only deterrent to prevent murder.
Before concluding, Mr. Speaker, I am sure that we all advocate the same objectives which is to provide more protection and better security to the public, but it is possible that we do not consider the same means.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the current wisdom is that parliament will pass Bill C-84 and thus abolish capital punishment, though probably by a very narrow majority. At the same time, sir, it is readily apparent that no issue in recent years has so aroused the Canadian public, the vast majority of whom, according to most indicators, favour retention. How can this apparent contradiction between the views of parliamentarians and those of the electorate be explained? Paradoxically, I believe it is probably because we are each talking and thinking about different things; some about deterrence and others about appropriate punishment. The latter consideration has been neglected by both sides, and probably to the detriment of each.
Those who oppose capital punishment tell us, correctly, that there is no conclusive evidence which demonstrates that the fear of death or the supreme penalty inhibits the potential murderer from killing. Abolitionists also argue the fact that some murderers have proven to be easier to rehabilitate than other types of criminals-and it is obviously true that you cannot rehabilitate a man after you have hanged him.
Such arguments would be entirely valid if those who sought to retain capital punishment wanted it to apply in all murder cases and if they based their argument on deterrence alone. Retentionists differ on the criteria they would apply in deciding when capital punishment is appropriate-although premeditated murder, or, in other words, murder for hire and the murder of police and prison guards are cited most frequently. However, most retentionists do not advocate supreme penalty for unpremeditated family murders, crimes of passion or murders committed because of quarrels among erstwhile friends. It is noteworthy that crimes of this type constitute by far the largest proportion of murders committed in this and other countries.
The retentionists accept, or I presume most do, that capital punishment would not be an effective deterrent in cases of this second type of murder. Moreover, I contend they believe that this type of crime, while reprehensible, is less vicious than those I enumerated first, in that with

May 25, 1976
Capital Punishment
respect to the first group of murderers the retentionist believes, not only that on some occasions the fear of being hanged will have the desired deterrent effect but that, even if it does not, capital punishment is the just punishment for the perpetrators of such crimes. If a person schemes, without extenuating circumstances of any kind, to deprive another person of his life for his own personal gain, then he deserves to receive the maximum penalty possible for his own iniquities.
We should, it is true, consider all diminutions of responsibility and all mitigating circumstances in determining the appropriate penalty. Hence, when there is full responsibility and no mitigating circumstances, the criminal should be treated with the full force of the law. Justice requires that punishment should fit the crime and the criminal. To be sure, there is no more fitting punishment than death for the person who plans to kill his business partner for financial gain. On the other hand, if we discover that the victim was having an affair with his murderer's spouse, we will agree that there are mitigating circumstances. It is precisely when there are no such circumstances that the death penalty for such crime becomes appropriate.
In order to persuade parliamentarians and the public to support the abolition of capital punishment, the government has introduced a punitive bill on prison sentences for murderers which will do little either to make society safer or to improve the quality of justice. The mandatory sentence to be served for first-degree murder is to be 25 years, and ten years for second-degree murder. When, and if, the cynical manoeuvring implicit in trading-off supposedly tougher laws regarding sentencing of murderers in return for the abolition of capital punishment ceases, then abolition will become more feasible. I say, with respect, sir, that there should be no trade-offs involving matters such as these.
The two main aspects of this bill contain contradictory principles, and as a result this legislation is offensive to retentionists and abolitionists alike. There are two questions involved in this bill, and I can see no reason that we cannot discuss them separately, based on their own respective merits. Let us consider, for example, the case of a 45-year old man convicted of first-degree murder. Under the presently proposed legislation, he will be incarcerated until he is 70 years of age. He has no incentive to improve; he is a constant escapee threat, notwithstanding the higher penalties for attempted escape, and a continuing danger to guards and other prisoners. But if the abolitionists are right, as I believe they are, that murderers without previous criminal records are among the easiest to rehabilitate, and if the criminal has not committed the kind of crime of the type I enumerated a few minutes ago, then to incarcerate such a man or person for 25 years is in itself a denial of justice. Here is a man who could probably contribute something to society, and our proposed new law would deny that possibility. Moreover, the government's negligible efforts at rehabilitation make the possibility of further rehabilitation more unlikely, even if the period of incarceration was lengthened.
The ten-year mandatory sentence for second-degree murder, with the judge's option of an extension of this sentence to 25 years, is probably even worse. Take, for
[Mr. MacKay.)
another example, the case of a woman who killed her husband intentionally in a fit of anger because he was constantly beating her and her children, or gambling and drinking away the family income. While we would scarcely consider such behaviour acceptable, it is doubtful that most people would consider it appropriate if she was incarcerated for a minimum of ten years. In each case, I believe the punishment should be determined by the specific circumstances of the crime and the previous record of the criminal. The proposed new legislation denies us the right to such elementary justice and, incidentally, casts doubt on the statement of the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) when he speaks of his dedication to a more civilized society.
I believe, strongly, in more judicial discretion and not in tying the hands of our judges with mandatory sentences, which in many cases could be exercised by people without any judicial training whatsoever and which, unfortunately, is becoming more and more a trend in our criminal jurisprudence; that is to say, taking away the right of the judge to decide in individual cases that which is right and appropriate and denying to society and those who appear before him the conscientious deliberation of one of those people in our society whose only mandate is to do the right thing.
The consequence of the proposed new law, if passed, will not merely be that capital punishment will be abolished, but that there will be much less true justice for those who are incarcerated. Moreover, the very real possibility exists that juries will refuse to convict when a minimum sentence seems too excessive.
Should members of parliament abolish capital punishment when its retention is desired by a majority of Canadians is a question which no doubt many members have asked themselves time after time during this debate. Parliamentarians are representatives of the people who elect them, not their delegates. According to the parliamentary tradition, members of parliament should decide on the basis of their wisdom and their conscience. While we should listen to our constituents, the final decision should be ours and not theirs. At this point I reject the self-serving assertions by some abolitionists that only they are following this honoured parliamentary tradition, and also the clear inference that the retentionists are somehow merely responding to the whim of the moment.
Parliamentarians should not mindlessly do what their constituents want. That is obvious. On the other hand, when they want to do something that is abhorrent to most of the people, they should be much more certain of their motives. Members of Parliament ought to be careful in overruling the clear and collective wishes of the people which, of course, in effect is the situation in considering this particular piece of legislation at this point in Canada's history.
I ask the government to withdraw or drastically modify this piece of legislation. As I said earlier, there are two distinct principles involved in this legislation. I believe members of this House must have the opportunity to decide each of the principles separately and according to their merits. In any event I, for one, shall vote according to
May 25, 1976

my conscience. I ask only that the Solicitor General and other abolitionists do the same and refrain from imputing motives to members who may not agree with their point of view.
Our existing criminal law over the centuries has been refined to the point where an accused does have sufficient protection to take into account practically all mitigating circumstances. In this country, when a person is accused of murder there is an assumption of innocence. In our system of criminal jurisprudence there is the right to a preliminary hearing, the right in respect of a grand jury, the right in respect of a petit jury, and the right of appeal right up to the Supreme Court of Canada in respect of any conviction, and in the final analysis, the possibility of the royal prerogative of mercy being exercised on behalf of the person concerned.
All these safeguards are in addition to the very real principle which has existed in our form of justice over the years, that of making sure that it is better for 100 guilty men to walk away than that one innocent man be convicted. All juries are instinctively aware of this tradition. All these safeguards exist, in addition to the option of being acquitted by reason of mental disability, of being convicted of lesser crimes, or included offences, such as manslaughter on the basis on self-defence, mistake or accidentally. Those of us who have practiced law realize, as the previous speaker said, that there is hardly any imaginable chance that in this day and age any person would be executed for a crime that was not of the most reprehensible and terrible type.
We have a system of criminal law and jurisprudence which has served us well. It can be modified and improved, that is for sure; but I am not convinced that the ultimate penalty at this point in time should not be maintained, to be used only in cases when there are no mitigating circumstances that could possibly be taken into account by conscientious jurists or by conscientious members of the cabinet.
To follow the thrust of this bill at this particular time in an attempt to make things more desirable or better for law enforcement in our society, I suggest is not feasible. If this legislation is supposed to be a cure for some sort of malady or disease that is affecting our society at this time because of the forces and influence of crime, it is a cure that I feel will be worse than the disease itself.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I feel somewhat honoured to be able to participate in this debate on Bill C-84 since we will be having a free vote on this very important matter. To begin, I should like to say that once again this House meets to debate and vote on a bill involving the issue of capital punishment. The last time the issue came before the House, in the fall of 1973, a measure was passed that saw the death penalty for a five-year period except in respect of those who had murdered policemen and prison guards. It should be pointed out that the result was the abolishment of the death penalty in all cases, since the government has shown itself to be utterly unwilling to apply the law as it stands. The government can argue that it has been completely within the letter of the law, that it has the power to commute any death sentence, but it is the spirit of the law that has been violated. It is satisfying to know we will see the end of the spectacle of a government
Capital Punishment
that frustrates the law of the land, whatever the fate of the bill as it now stands. In other words, we will finally see the law carried out one way or the other regardless of how people across the country feel.
In the bill before us we are asked to vote for total abolition of the death penalty in Canada. This I cannot do. In fact, I cannot support any legislation on this matter which does not include the death penalty, as potential punishment, not only for the killing of policemen and prison guards but for all premeditated murder. In taking my position, I do not picture myself as a vengeful, bloodthirsty ogre, but as a responsible member of parliament making a decision that is true to both my conscience and the sentiments of most of my constituents. The decision was taken only after weighing all the factors as I saw them.
I have no great emotional attachment to the death penalty as such, as has been expressed by people throughout the various parts of the country and by some members of this parliament. If an alternative were to appear that I felt was as effective for the protection of society, I would support it. However, due to the unique nature of capital punishment as a deterrent, it is doubtful such an alternative can be found. Capital punishment cannot be dismissed as a simplistic solution. The alternative certainly has not been provided in the mandatory 25-year sentence for premeditated murder found in Bill C-84. This measure is a carrot-on-the-end-of-a-stick approach by the government. In the past, when the government knew it could not get a majority in favour of total abolition, it compromised by making exceptions for the murderers of policemen and prison guards' and by restricting the measure to five years. Now, when the move has been made to total abolition, the 25-year minimum sentence has, in my opinion, been thrown in to pull enough votes to the abolition side in an attempt to ensure passage.
My position on capital punishment is not based on any philosophy of "an eye for an eye" but a desire-and I hope a sincere desire-to protect society, something that is not obvious today. We have been told that use of the death penalty would brutalize civilization. I not only dispute this claim but I suggest that capital punishment is necessary if we are to prevent civilization from becoming more brutal and lawless.
To my way of thinking, capital punishment as a deterrent has two aspects. The first is that the threat of the potential use of the death penalty deters a certain segment of the criminal or potentially criminal population from using murder to accomplish their ends. The second is that carrying out the death penalty in those cases where there is no hope of rehabilitation and the chance of further acts of violence, including murder, seem likely, capital punishment is the ultimate deterrent.
I am not going to quote statistics in support of my position that capital punishment does have a deterrent effect. That has been done, ad nauseum, on both sides of this issue until the figures become meaningless. For example, the retentionist side can point to the rising murder rate since partial abolition in 1967, which in practice under this government has been total abolition, and the abolition-

Capital Punishment
ists can quickly point out the rising numbers of all crimes, implying that the rise in the murder rate has little or nothing to do with abolition but is just a reflection of a general increase in crime across Canada and certainly in most countries of the world.
Which view of the statistics is correct? I really do not think that question can be answered, because once again it depends strictly on the way in which you use statistics. Thus, my reluctance to use statistics in support of my argument is not because such statistics are not available but because I recognize that the other side can support their argument equally well with a different interpretation or set of statistics, thus putting us no further ahead.
The use of deterrents is well recognized in our judicial system. It is one of the prime motives behind the principle of lesser penalties for lesser crimes. As murder, especially premedidated murder, must be considered the ultimate crime, should not society impose the ultimate penalty-not for vengeance but for its own defence?
I would like to say a few words on the aspect of public opinion on this issue, and certainly the House of Commons as the forum which we are using to debate this piece of legislation is the focal point of public opinion which is shifting back and forth across the country. I certainly hope I am not one of those people who wish to see this or any other issue decided by public referendum. I would certainly like to state that in my view that would be an abdication of the responsibility of parliament to make the laws for Canadian society. If we used the method of public referendum, we could do this with any number of pieces of legislation. However, in any issue public opinion, especially when it is as clearly defined as it is in this case, must be given some weight in each member's decision. My sympathy goes to those members who must choose between the wishes of the large majority of their constituents and their own personal view. Fortunately, I have no such difficult decision. The vast majority of my constituents, and myself, are in agreement on the necessity of the retention of capital punishment, though not always for the same reasons.
The coverage by the media of this issue seems to imply that the only members following their conscience are those who favour abolition. I want to make the point emphatically that the members in favour of abolition do not have a monopoly on voting by conscience, as the media would have us believe. Many-I believe, the vast majority-of those voting against the bill do so because of their own personal beliefs. That public opinion shares these beliefs in no way alters the fact that these members will be voting true to their conscience, just as will many of those members supporting the bill. If those sections of the media that are pressing members whose personal views conflict with those of their constituents to vote in accordance with their conscience wish to be consistent, should that same principle not also apply to those close retentionists in the cabinet who are being forced to toe the line on this issue?
In Bill C-83 and Bill C-84 the government has supposedly provided us with its definitive statement on violent crime. However, the measures contained in the legislation leave significant gaps in the areas of prevention and rehabilitation. For example, no measures have been proposed to deal with the significant incidence of hard drug
[Mr. Murta.l
related crime, or with the problems of crime among Canada's native population. These problems need special attention which one does not find in the peace and security legislation or in this bill.
I would now like to explain what I feel is the increased danger when a mandatory 25-year sentence is combined with abolition of the death penalty.

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I appreciate the fact that private members' hour will be suspended today to allow us to continue this very important debate. As I was saying before the interruption, I would like to explain what I feel is the increased danger when a mandatory, 25-year sentence is combined with abolition of the death penalty. This increased danger will focus on two law enforcement groups that in the present law are given special status. Consider what will likely be a common case should this bill pass-a murderer sentenced to 25 years in prison, but secure in his knowledge that he cannot be executed no matter what his crime is in the future. Will not the number of attempts at escaping increase when a prisoner is faced with 25 years in confinement, as opposed to, let us say, 10 years? Will not the level of violence used in these more frequent escape attempts be higher when the prisoner is faced with a penalty of only further imprisonment?
Would not a similar response be expected of a successful escapee avoiding recapture? We have enough incidents of escapes and hostage-taking in our penitentiary system at present, without bringing in measures which are sure to increase their number and severity. These problems, these fears, have been borne out by various law enforcement agencies across the country in virtually every province in Canada. From a position of providing special protection for law enforcement officers-at least in theory-we are now being asked to vote in favour of measures which will increase the already substantial risks to which they are exposed. Many of these law enforcement officers are very concerned about the outcome of this legislation if the bill passes as it has been presented by the government.
In conclusion, let me deal with the concept of cruel and unusual punishment. I cannot imagine how any member of parliament can argue that condemning a man to 25 years in our present penal system is an act of mercy, compared with the death penalty. In their zeal to placate their own consciences, many hon. members may be sentencing men to
May 25, 1976

fates far worse than death. Anyone who has had a chance to look at our present penal system certainly must agree.
In my opinion, this legislation is a poor answer to a very complex problem and cannot do anything but make things worse, not only for policemen and prison guards but also for law-abiding citizens across Canada. The most serious effect of the legislation in Bill C-84 and also in Bill C-83- which I suppose we can consider as one piece of peace and security legislation-is that we have not started down the road to any meaningful reform of our penal system at all. When this debate is over, we will go back to what we had before, and unfortunately the issues may not arise again for a long period of time. What we have done is perpetuate a system which has demonstrated that it is just not working.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the position I took in this House on February 20, 1973 concerning the abolition or the retention of the death penalty remains the same. This is not surprising since the reforms on crime prevention that I would have wanted to see brought forward have not been forthcoming, unfortunately, so that it is impossible for me today to approve the abolition of the death penalty simply because, to my mind, society's protection would be harmed by such a measure.
Indeed, there are criminals. We are concerned about punishing them through forced labour, imprisonment and hanging. In any event, we are not concerned about healing the causes which drive some individuals to crime. In the social sector, much has been done but there is still much to be done. With our present education system, we are preparing criminals.
In the report which we have been given and which is written by Dr. Fattah, a criminologist from British Columbia, we find on pages 147, 151 and 165 tables which show that among the people surveyed 50 to 60 per cent believe that discipline in schools is not strict enough; this was the opinions of primary and secondary students as much as of adults aged from 20 to 39, 30 to 49, 50 or more. The lack of discipline produces criminals.
In 1968, the Divorce Act was amended, but the regulations concerning the maintenance rules allow one spouse to have a coercive power over the other. As we read on pages 32 and 33 of Working Paper 12 by the Law Reform Commission of Canada on "Maintenance on divorce", and I quote:
It is an unfortunate part of the folklore of marriage, because of the legal tradition involved here, that the "innocent" husband should be able to put the "guilty" wife "out on the street without a penny", and when the situation is reversed, the wife should be able to "take him for every cent he's got."
In most divorce cases the wife is automatically responsible for children. If she finds a job, she will have to pay a baby sitter, but according to the statistics of the Royal Commission on the Status of Women, one sees that generally her salary will not be sufficient for her to adopt such a solution. The only alternative left to her will be social welfare which will be just enough, if not to live, to survive. If she dares pay a lawyer to seek a maintenance allowance from her husband, there will be a ruling of course but how can it be enforced since she is given no coercive means to make him pay alimony?
Capital Punishment
In that respect, I hope that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) who is now studying if it is possible to pay maintenance allowances, will be able to bring forward such a humanitarian policy. To conclude, with entire families living in a state of constant humiliation and poverty, the Senate commission proved that the state of poverty tends to lead directly to crime. In days of yore, we might have been able to suggest that the poor try to recapture in work some of the dignity they lost, but because of current high unemployment, which seems to show a tendency to increase instead of decrease, our solution would not be welcome!
Unemployment strikes like a plague: the young people, without preparation, the drop-outs, soon become young delinquents; the graduates, become our unemployed with degrees. I know a forest engineer with many degrees who has been looking for a job for two years now, and is still looking. People of 40 or more are considered less productive that the young and women. The latter are the least disadvantaged in the labour market, very often because they accept jobs the men would not do for the money offered.
If that continues, we will soon be running short of taxpayers and workers to pay for unemployment benefits. We will then have achieved the real society of leisure, won't we? But, all that compulsory leisure called "unemployment", Mr. Speaker, finally leads to crime.
As a consequence of all those weeknesses in the fundamental systems that govern our Canadian society, we witness high juvenile delinquency rates and criminality that the judicial system does not remedy. We have reached the point where we invoke judicial error as the reason for abolishing the death penalty. We fear judicial errors, Mr. Speaker, but who commits those errors? Certainly not the one who was killed, who was its victim.
Neither by the accused who may also be the victim of this error. By the members of the jury? But if they make a miscarriage of justice, they cannot be held responsible for that since they are also in some way victims of it. There remains only our judicial system to blame. Perjury, forging of evidence, conjuring of witnesses produce miscarriage of justice at the beginning of the chain, and our antiquated and inadequate penitentiary and rehabilitation system closes the ring of injustices. Unable to correct them, we imagine being able to prevent them by trading off the death penalty for life imprisonment.
I have here a document dated June 26, 1973 and signed by inmates from Cowansville. The prisoners themselves do not accept this solution. They say that even though you are against capital punishment and your vote makes the balance turn towards abolition, nothing will change if in exchange you accept the implementation of a prolonged punishment which under a more humane disguise will only be a death by inches. To deny all hope to prisoners means they will become madmen, dangerous people for those they live with or even leading them to suicide.
And it seems they are right, Mr. Speaker, if we are to believe the statistics on the number of suicides among prisoners in federal institutions. Between 1959 and 1965, when capital punishment was enforced, there were 27 suicides. Between 1965 and 1972, after capital punishment was suspended, there were 77. Prisoners advocate what they

Capital Punishment
call "preventive detention", a formula which would be more like rehabilitation than punishment and which, in my opinion, would deserve closer study. But we are not talking about prevention, but punishment, are we not, Mr. Speaker?
As things now stand, we will have to be very strict. Even some members of the Parole Board are of that opinion. Mrs. Mary Lynch, who retired last November 26 after 15 years in that service stated before the press that it might not yet be the moment to abolish hanging in Canada.
Some people will retort that moral authorities, namely churches, have just decided against the retention of capital punishment. Personally I think that this position by bishops is ambiguous because they do not deny the state the right to impose capital punishment if required by circumstances. But this is the case and we infer that when required by circumstances, the death penalty must be applied.
The League for Human Rights itself determined two objectives: protect society and rehabilitate the murderer. In its document of January 31, 1973, it says:
It is necessary for Canadian society to have maximum protection against murderers . .. and ... it is fair for society to force the murderer to make up for his act.
There I say, Mr. Speaker, that because society has not yet provided the appropriate prevention and protection mechanisms, we have no alternative other than voting for the retention of capital punishment.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to echo a few of the sentiments expressed by some of my colleagues today about the importance of this debate at this time. The government has been stressing that they want to get the business of the House completed as soon as possible and yet they bring on a debate which, as far as I can see, at this moment has very little importance.
This is the second time that I have had the opportunity to participate in this debate, Mr. Speaker, and neither of these instances would have been necessary if the government had tended to its business. Just over three years ago, on May 16, 1973, was the first time I contributed to the debate on capital punishment. The reason I say it is not necessary that I should have participated at all is that at that time the bill had already expired. The government had lacked the foresight to introduce replacing legislation prior to the end of 1972 when the first partial ban on capital punishment expired. The debate in 1973 extended the partial ban on capital punishment to December, 1977, some 20 months from today. I say there was plenty of time for the government to have organized its program so that the debate could have taken place at a time when the pressure of House business was not so intensive.
My stand, however, does not demand capital punishment in any spirit of blood lust or revenge. The argument I hope to develop will stress the fact that society needs protection by the government-it needs protection from the government, too-I suspect-Mr. Speaker. However, protection of the public is the point I want to stress as being the most
[Mr. Guay (Levis).l
important. Before I get into that, however, there is another factor I should like to discuss. This bill presents a "no loss" situation to the abolitionists. In other words, if the bill is passed by the House, then we will have abolition and they will have won the day. On the other hand, if the bill is defeated, it will simply mean that we will continue with the law that exists at the present time and in fact we will still be without capital punishment because for the last 14 years this government has practised abolition.
We should look at the law as it stands so that we will know the alternatives if the bill is defeated. Apparently recognizing the vulnerability of police and prison guards, and probably realizing that it was a necessary feature to get the last bill passed, the government included a provision that killers of police or prison guards shall be or can be executed. Of course, the cabinet retained the power to commute the death sentence and that is the practice they have followed.
I do not think there is anyone in this House on either side of the issue who would not agree with the proposition that murderers should be removed from society, if not permanently then certainly for a very long time. In some cases, that would be extended until they were cured of their propensity to murder. When we are considering murder and the punishment therefor, I think it is important to define exactly what we mean by the term "murder." After all, many offences that involve killing are not murder and the perpetrator is not subject to the ultimate penalty. I should like to read a definition I came across in a Globe and Mail editorial of February 26:
First degree murder is defined in the bill as planned and deliberate murder and as the killing of a police officer, prison guard or a person working in a prison even though the killing was not planned and deliberate. It would also be first degree murder, even though not planned and deliberate, if someone were killed during the hijacking of an aircraft, or during a kidnapping, rape, attempted rape or an indecent assault on a male or on a female.
Those are all heinous crimes, Mr. Speaker, and I am certain there will be agreement that the ultimate penalty should be imposed for them. Where we have some difficulty is with the so-called passion killing or other "heat of the battle" type killings. I do not think most people want to see the perpetrators executed, and that is where some of our difficulties arise. I think some who are abolitionists have arrived at their conclusion, because they fear a miscarriage of justice, that the wrong person will be executed and society will be unable to make it up to him. I am not certain how well we can make up an error after a man has served 25 years. It would be very difficult to restore those 25 years to him if he were found to be innocent or to have been erroneously convicted.
Dealing with the error aspect, I should like to read a paragraph from a letter I received from Hon. J. V. Clyne, a resident of Vancouver. Mr. Clyne is a retired industrialist and, what makes him more unusual, a retired jurist. He resigned from the Supreme Court of British Columbia in order to return to industry, in which he embarked on another successful career. He wrote the following to me:
You know the elaborate precautions which are taken to make certain that the accused is deemed to be innocent until found guilty and is deserving of death. It is necessary for the Crown to prove intent in
May 25, 1976

order for a man to be found guilty of murder. If intent is not proved but death ensues as a result of a criminal act then the charge is reduced to manslaughter. It is likewise reduced to manslaughter even if the accused formed the intent to kill but acted on the instant under extreme provocation and the degree of provocation is for the jury to consider. It may likewise be reduced to manslaughter if the jury finds that the accused acted reasonably in self-defence. The judge must always charge the jury in a criminal action that the Crown must prove its case beyond reasonable doubt and if the defence raises a reasonable doubt in the jury's mind it must either acquit or reduce the charge. I mention these matters to emphasize that every safeguard is taken to prevent a miscarriage of justice.
I shall refer to that letter later. What he said ought to allay some fears. After all, society and governments must make decisions from time to time. Existing safeguards against accidental or erroneous convictions are of a high standard.
Many hon. members have referred to the opinions of their constituents. I want to do the same and to refer to other opinions as well. Like many colleagues in the House, I sent a questionnaire to constituents. In 1974, after passage of existing legislation, I asked my constituents the following question, among others: "Are you in favour of capital punishment for other murderers as well as for murderers of police or prison guards?" In other words, the implication was: "You are stuck with this law for the next four or five years; do you think it goes far enough, or should it go further?" We received 3,248 responses, which represent a return of 13 per cent. Statisticians consider a response of about 6 per cent as normal. I think, as we received double the normal response, that we did fairly well, although I do not think one can assume from the greater than normal response that one side or the other would express a stronger opinion.
The result was that 75 per cent of the residents of my riding expressed themselves as being in favour of capital punishment for other murderers as well as for murderers of police or prison guards. If hon. members consider the definition of "murder" to which I referred previously, it will help them to think more clearly.
Society entrusts the enforcement of its laws to the police. Admittedly, at times the police have a difficult job to do. I do not know why abolitionists seem unable to pay much attention to the views of the police, to whom they entrust the enforcement of the laws. I therefore refer hon. members to what the Canadian Police Association wrote to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) last year. In part, the letter said:
The association is deeply concerned over the fact that there is now no penalty of consequence on persons who commit murder in our country. Persons convicted of murder who are given a "life" sentence can be eligible for parole in seven to ten years after conviction. It is the view of the policemen of this country, as represented by the association, that this is not a suitable penalty and does not serve to protect society.
The view has been expressed that juries tend not to convict if they feel that a conviction will mean putting the accused to death. On the other side of the argument there is the equal danger that the policeman under fire or the pressure of his job will, perhaps unknowingly or unconsciously, develop a tendency to act without benefit of law. In other words, he may take the law into his own hands. Faced with the choice of making a difficult capture or killing in action, it is possible he will take the law unto himself and act accordingly. That will not be the honourable thing for him to do; he may do it even without
Capital Punishment
realizing what he is doing. The point is that the government will put him in such a position that he will be under those pressures.
I shall now refer to something an official of the John Howard Society said. I am sure hon. members appreciate the good work the John Howard Society has done for many years. A member of the board of directors said he would rather "they hang murderers than see them imprisoned with very little chance of coming out." We know that the suggested alternative to capital punishment is the long prison term, perhaps of 25 years. The John Howard Society has long been an advocate of rehabilitation, but it knows, from its experience, that a 25-year prison term will preclude any hope of rehabilitation. It suggests capital punishment is better than 25 years in jail.
Hon. members have received much correspondence from churches. I have a letter from the Canadian Council of Churches; it is addressed to me. The letter speaks of "the following bodies" as having spoken in favour of the abolition of capital punishment. Various churches are listed, including the Anglican Church in Canada which is at the top of the list, the Baptist, Presbyterian and Mennonite churches, the Roman Catholic church, the Society of Friends and the United Church of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I have some support in the House. It is all very well for a body to establish a policy, but I do not think they should try to impose their will on the members of the church who have not been consulted on a matter. It is not even as if they were outvoted; they were not even consulted on the issue.
I note that the Baptist church takes a somewhat different position, and I point out that the list previously alluded to contains the Baptist convention of Ontario and Quebec. I have in my possession a letter from a Baptist minister in my riding, Vancouver Quadra. The Reverend Wald Krogu-letz is in favour of capital punishment, but did not try to foist his views on his parishioners. I wish to quote a paragraph from the letter. It reads:
Most politicians who quote the sixth commandment: "Thou shalt not kill", have little or no theological understanding of the true meaning of the same. This divine law forbids any individual to hatefully and planfully murder any other individual. The sixth commandment does not prohibit the state to punish and execute the offending criminal-
He makes a reference to Exodus which I shall not repeat now. I shall be saying something later about the right and duty of the state to afford the protection to which I have alluded.

May 25, 1976
Capital Punishment
In the last debate we heard a speech by an Anglican clergyman who was an M.P. of this party. I thought he summed things up very well. In fact I sent copies of that speech out to a number of people who wrote to me concerning capital punishment. In a key paragraph of that speech in 1973 he said:
The conviction is growing among a great number of Canadians that we need the death penalty as one way of reversing the permissive trend of the past decade ... Few citizens of this country find much pleasure in the sight or thought of a fellow human being hanged. But there are many who want some assurance that the law is going to be enforced and that the public is going to be protected. They do not want cruelty shown to anybody but they want the ordinary man, woman and child of this country protected and they want to say to the criminal element of this society that that element is on notice that society is prepared to defend itself.
A lot has been said about the deterrent effect of capital punishment. There is probably no way of proving that capital punishment is a deterrent, or that it is not. I have heard it said that it is certainly a deterrent to repeaters, and I agree with that obvious statement. It is unfortunate we do not have statistics to lend weight to one side of the argument or the other. As hon. members know, capital punishment has not been carried out in this country since 1963, so both sides of the case cannot be argued. The contention that capital punishment is not a deterrent is not a very strong one when we bear in mind that capital punishment has not been enforced for so long a period.
It is accepted, I presume, that penalties of one kind or another do act as a deterrent otherwise there would be little point, for example, in imposing fines for parking offences-and we find that a three dollar penalty nowadays is not particularly effective as a deterrent; indeed we find parking offences committed all over the place. Nevertheless our selection of punishment ranges all the way up to long prison sentences for serious crimes such as assault and robbery, right up to death for murder. If it can be said with certainty that the death penalty is not a deterrent to murder, how can it be argued that life imprisonment is a deterrent? Indeed, why should we concern ourselves with punishment of any kind?
Even in British Columbia where a socialist government decided that traffic fines favour the rich and should therefore be abolished, there is still a deterrent to dangerous or careless motoring. Indeed, it is probably more of a deterrent than the previous penalties. Offenders are now awarded demerit points, and after a certain number of demerit points they lose their licences.
I should like to refer to an article which appeared in a magazine called The Canadian Police Chief, written by one Sid Nelson, and appearing in the issue of January, 1976, He talks about deterrence in these terms:
The question of deterrence is secondary to the question of justice and we ought not to confuse the two. One person has observed, however, that capital punishment is really the ultimate deterrent in that it assures us that he who has murdered another will never murder again. A prominent lawyer in Montreal has affirmed that an escaped murderer who was his client probably killed five other persons on his escape. In this instance capital punishment would have saved the lives of five other people.
I consider this to be a very strong argument although it is evidently one which has not been accepted by the government. Talking about the protection of the public, which is my main theme, I say that if a murderer is sentenced to

life imprisonment or to 25 years in prison it means he will be there for the rest of his useful life. There is no deterrent for him not to stay in prison. In other words there is every encouragement for him to attempt to escape. If he kills people getting out or if he kills people while he is outside the worst punishment he faces is to go back to jail for the rest of his life. But he is already there for the rest of his life, and after all one can only serve one life sentence.
I maintain that the work of prison guards and of police officers becomes increasingly difficult and dangerous in times when the the death penalty is not carried out. As I say, prisoners find themselves in a "no-loss" situation- somewhat the same as the government finds itself in presently. Prisoners are likely to make use of every occasion and every means possible to escape and find their way back to the free world.
I also want to say something about the power of the state to execute. Some people assert that the state does not have the right to take human life. I suggest that the evidence on the other side of the question is stronger. In my view, not only does the state have the power to protect citizens and execute others in the course of carrying out that protection but it has a duty to protect innocent members of the public.
The state abrogates its duty if it refuses to execute people in cases where such a penalty is obviously warranted. I would refer members who are concerned about this aspect to consider what happens when the state declares war on an enemy of the state. In effect, by declaring war, the state gives a licence to members of the armed forces to kill. It makes very little difference whether we are concerned with an enemy of the state during wartime, such as the second world war, or with an enemy of the state in the shape of an isolated individual murderer. The state has a duty to protect, and it cannot protect the public if it declines to use a power which it now possesses under the law.
I realize there are some who are abolitionists because they object to the method of execution used. I am not one who would insist that hanging is the only way or even the best way in which executions should be carried out. Once again I refer to the letter from J. V. Clyne of Vancouver and read these few sentences:
When I was on the bench I did make certain investigations regarding the gas chamber and the electric chair and on the basis of making death quick and effective I think hanging is a better choice than either of them. I believe however that there should be substituted in modern times a form of euthanasia, that is to say, the means of procuring a quiet and easy death. With the advancement in the knowledge of drugs this should not be difficult. As I have said the death penalty should be preserved but there should be an enquiry as to the means of carrying it out.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, may I summarize my remarks. My investigation leads me to the conclusion that Canada needs capital punishment at this time. The present abuse of the will of parliament by the cabinet is seriously undermining public respect for the law. The public must be assured of protection of the law and by the law. I urge my colleagues in the House to oppose this bill as a step on the road to these overdue changes.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think this is the third time I have participated in a debate
May 25, 1976

on this subject since I have been in this House. I must say I think all sides on this particular issue should be congratulated on the rational nature of the debate. I think it has maintained a rather high standard, in the sense that I do not hear too many of those who are abolitionists calling the one side bloodthirsty, and I do not hear those on the other side calling the abolitionists yellow and so on, so in a sense I think the debate is a worth-while one.
Before getting into the question of the death penalty itself I want to deal briefly with the bill and the alternative proposed in the bill, that of a 25 year mandatory sentence for first degree murder. We have had quite a bit of comment about this being a trade-off and so on. The facts are that under section 672(1), as I read the bill, the mandatory nature of the sentence is 15 years, not 25 years. The chief justice of a province has the authority, and I think the duty to appoint three of his judges to sit not merely to make recommendations back to the parole board but to make decisions on how much longer the mandatory section of a sentence is to last. To those who are on the side of arguing that 25 years is a more draconian alternative than the death penalty I suggest they look carefully at this bill.
I think the government should be subject to some criticism for using the argument about a trade-off. Any examination of the bill clearly leads one to the conclusion that the mandatory sentence for first degree murder is 15 years, not 25 years, and I cannot understand why the media and the public are talking about a sentence of 25 years. People in prison who have had the 25 year sentence imposed on them, once they have served 15 years of their sentence will clearly be able to make a routine application to the chief justice of the province, and the chief justice will routinely appoint three judges who will make the sort of decision that the parole board has been making up until now, so I do not think we should kid the public about what this bill really provides.
As for the other issue, the question of capital punishment, we have had this time more than a dialogue between the deaf. Most of the time when we get into this kind of debate we always assume our positions are entirely fixed, that no one will budge from matters of conscience which may have been developed over many years. However, I think in fact some listening is going on. I do not know how much change there has been in terms of debate, but the thrust of the argument has changed. For example, those who are advocating abolition are emphasizing questions that deal with the safety of the public rather than whether we live in a civilized society and such philosophical questions as that. I should like to spend some of my time on whether public safety is enhanced through the use of the death penalty or whether in fact its use increases public risk.
Some of the new evidence that has come forward on this subject has to do with the murder rate. Those who argue for retention have some evidence that we should certainly consider, namely, that the murder rate has doubled since between 1962 and 1974. In 1962 the rate was 1.2 per thousand; it is now 2.4 per thousand, using constant population figures. This is a significant change and well worth examination, no matter which side of the question one is on. It is
Capital Punishment
clear that it is not just public imagination that says that rates of crime and murder are increasing.
I would ask those who favour retention of the death penalty on those grounds to consider the fact that the department of vital statistics disclosed that in 1961, when hanging was in vogue, 20 per cent of criminal homicides led to charges of manslaughter, whereas in 1974 only 7 per cent were manslaughter. What, in effect, has happened is that the murder statistics have risen, not entirely but partly, as a result of the police laying more murder charges. The reason that more murder charges tend to be laid is that the chances of conviction are higher when the death penalty is not the penalty facing the jury when they make their ultimate decision. In terms of statistical evidence murder has increased, but I do not think it has increased quite as dramatically as the bald figures themselves disclose.
The media have some responsibility for the public's perception of its own safety and the risk that the public itself on an average basis faces. There is no question in my mind that anyone who watches a great deal of television has a different perception from those who do not expose themselves to the myriad of media violence to which we are continually exposed. I want to quote briefly from "Psychology Today" for April, 1976, which has an article dealing with the perception of crime and personal safety and how this is affected by watching television. As a result of a very comprehensive study the article says;
We have found that people who watch a lot of TV see the real world as more dangerous, and frightening than those who watch very little. Heavy viewers are less trustful of their fellow citizens, and more fearful of the real world ...
In order to complete a story entertainingly in only an hour or even a half hour, conflicts on TV are usually personal and solved by action. Since violence is dramatic, and relatively simple to produce, much of the action tends to be violent.. . More than half of all characters on prime-time TV are involved in some violence, about one tenth in killing... Among those TV males with identifiable occupations, about 20 per cent are engaged in law enforcement. In the real world, the proportion runs less than one per cent...
Violence on television leads viewers to perceive the real world as more dangerous than it really is, which must also influence the way people behave. When asked, "Can most people be trusted?" the heavy viewers were 35 per cent more likely to check "Can't be too careful."
The conclusion of this study, which was quite extensive, is as follows:
We have found that violence on prime-time network TV cultivates exaggerated assumptions about the threat of danger in the real world. Fear is a universal emotion, and easy to exploit. The exaggerated sense of risk and insecurity may lead to increasing demands for protection, and to increasing pressure for the use of force by established authority.
The media have something else to account for, and that is whether public behaviour itself is affected in individual cases; for examples, whether a brain damaged individual or an individual with lower degrees of resistance to what he is seeing is influenced in terms of his potential for crime. When one looks at some of the more notorious crimes that have taken place involving murder, they are surprisingly close to actual media presentations. I am thinking now of a case that happened recently in the United States, and I read from the Ottawa Citizen of Friday, May 14, as follows:
David McRae, Jr., whose mother said he always wanted to be a policeman, walked into a bar in a seedy area Thursday and fatally shot

May 25, 1976
Capital Punishment
four persons after warning he was coming to clean out pimps, prostitutes, homosexuals and dope pushers.
I do not know whether they asked this individual, David McRae, what movies he had been seeing lately, but if he went to see a movie called "Taxi Driver" that is exactly what he would have seen in that picture. This is not just a coincidence. There are a number of very interesting murders which took place following the exposure to media violence of some person of low resistance or with possible brain damage, but with the potential for violence. It is too often that this sort of thing happens not long after such exposure.
The media have to start cleaning their own house or this place is going to start cleaning it. I think the time has come to examine the amount of violence to which we are exposing the public. Guidelines will have to be developed in the long run if the media do not develop their own guidelines.
We are dealing with a very sensitive area. The average person may not be affected, but if you take the typical serious criminal, and that is the individual who normally has failed at home or his home has failed him, has failed in school or his school has failed him, or has failed with his peer group or that group has failed him, where does he go? He sits at home watching television every day and thinks the whole world is flying to Hawaii and having a great time. He is sitting there with this sense of frustration, and when he is exposed to a film such as that movie "Taxi Driver", or other dramatic cases of crime, he then says, "I am going to go out and get some attention. I am going to get my piece of the action."
It is long overdue that we took a very careful look at some legislative guidelines regarding the kind of violence in the media to which we expose our children and other members of the public.
Let me now turn again to the question of capital punishment. After looking at the evidence and after considering the question of safety to the public, and I may say that I have studied it as intensively as I can, I am still of the opinion that there is no place for the death penalty, not only because it may not be worthy of the kind of civilization we are living in-and I do not believe that out of any sense of arrogance or moral superiority-but because there is no evidence that it will provide a deterrent, and there is no evidence that it will reduce the number of murders in our society. In fact the evidence is the other way. There is a considerable body of very persuasive evidence that the death penalty increases the murder rate by exposing the public to the risk of murderers being acquitted by juries who apply the standards of our criminal law which have been so time honoured.
The hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) indicated this afternoon, in favour of the principle of retention, that the safety valves within our judicial system are so extensive the capacity for error is almost infinitesimal or minimal. The facts are that when we examine some of the more dramatic cases which have led to a more widespread call by the public for a return of the death penalty, and some of the cases of the past, we still have the very uncomfortable feeling that we may have gotten the wrong man. Let me give you a couple of examples.
I suppose one of the most famous cases took place in my own riding, the case of the murder of Tanya Busch, the
[Mr. Leggatt.l
daughter of a guard. A man called Head was charged with the murder. It was a particularly vicious, rotten, and violent thing. In this case there was no eyewitness, and I believe two of the Crown witnesses changed their stories. There was no confession. I ask the public and I ask this House to consider whether, given those facts, and given the warning that a judge usually has to give the jury to satisfy itself beyond a reasonable doubt that the circumstances are not only consistent with the guilt but inconsistent with any other rational conclusion, even with capital punishment, that jury would have in fact convicted Gary Head of that murder. In the Saskatoon murders a similar situation occurred. This involves the whole question of dealing as an individual with a case rather than as a group of 200 people who may say, "Yes, bring back the death penalty because that is clearly the right answer." When you have 12 men sitting on a jury they start to act very differently. They assess the evidence, as it is their duty to do.
I can tell you that without exception those lawyers who have been involved in any kind of extensive criminal practice on the defence side will indicate that they prefer the death penalty if their purpose is to obtain an acquittal. The problem continues to be that a jury of 12 looks at a man for up to two weeks, and then has to make the decision.
I do not think we should do anything to abandon the jury system. It works and it works extremely well, but with the death penalty it works less well. The chance for an error by the jury, and the chance of acquittal of a person who is a murderer and who should be taken away from the public for its protection, with the death penalty in place in fact work in reverse to the detriment of the public.
The death penalty is not a deterrent. If you look at those societies which from time immemorial have continued to use the death penalty you will find they are consistently less safe than the one in which we are living. For instance, let us take Brazil, Spain, and Argentina. In Spain they impose the death penalty. In fact they have a vigilante gang running around imposing the death penalty in Brazil, and that does not help their society.
The public is entitled to some solution, but the problem with this long debate on the death penalty is that it deflects our judgment and our attention away from the cause of crime. As long as we continue to agonize on the death penalty or no death penalty we are wasting time in the sense that we should be dealing with what is happening within our society, trying to find out why it is tearing apart and why we have this dramatic increase in all kinds of crime. The fact is that we have done little or nothing about drug abuse. A large percentage of violent crime is related to the drug trade and we have done nothing about it. We have done nothing about alcohol. We continue to sell alcohol and governments continue to support themselves from the revenue.
May I call it six o'clock?
